key_terms.meaning: Computing by a user who is moving, delivered by a device, a wireless link, and a fixed network with middleware.
The wireless link between the mobile device and the nearest base station or access point.
Software sitting between the network and the app that hides mobility, disconnection and low bandwidth.
Using the same channel group in cells far enough apart that co-channel interference stays tolerable.
Number of cells after which a channel group repeats; N = i² + ij + j².
Q = D/R = √(3N), where D is the distance between co-channel cells and R is the cell radius.
Moving an active call from one base station to another without dropping it.
Location update reports where an idle user is; paging searches a group of cells when a call arrives.
Home Location Register: the database holding a subscriber's permanent record and current VLR address.
Visitor Location Register: temporary records of subscribers currently inside one MSC area.
Router on the mobile node's home network that stores its binding and forwards packets to it.
A temporary IP address that says where a mobile node is currently reachable.
The association of a home address with a care-of address, kept in the home agent's binding cache.
Packets travel CN → HA → MN even when CN and MN are close, so the path is longer than needed.
Listen before transmit, then back off randomly; optional RTS/CTS reserves the channel to avoid collisions.
A Bluetooth network of one master and up to seven active slaves hopping together on one channel.
Two or more piconets overlapping, with a node acting as a bridge between them.
Mobile nodes that route each other's packets with no base station and no fixed backbone.
Packet-switched data added on top of GSM, using SGSN and GGSN nodes.
Wideband CDMA, the 5 MHz radio interface used by UMTS.

takeaways: Mobile computing needs four things together: a device, a wireless link, a fixed network and middleware; remove one and the problem changes completely.
Each cellular generation added exactly one big capability: analog voice, then digital voice and SMS, then packet data, then broadband all-IP.
GSM carries voice on circuits, GPRS overlays packet switching on the same network, and UMTS replaces only the radio with WCDMA.
Frequency reuse is what makes cellular work: N = i² + ij + j² sets how far co-channel cells sit, and Q = √(3N) sets the interference.
Mobility management is two jobs: handover keeps a call alive, and location update plus paging keeps an idle user findable.
Mobile IP keeps one permanent home address and forwards packets through a tunnel to the care-of address; triangle routing is its main inefficiency.
IEEE 802.11 shares the radio with CSMA/CA and RTS/CTS, while Bluetooth organises nearby devices into a piconet under one master.
In a MANET every node is also a router, so the routing protocol, not the radio, is the hard design problem.
bank_note: Long answers here are usually built on diagrams plus one calculation: a labelled architecture drawing, a step-by-step signalling flow, and a frequency-reuse or capacity number worked out with units.

bank.q: Define mobile computing. Explain the three parts of its structure with a labelled diagram, and give two Indian applications.
outline: Definition: a user computes while moving, not just a small computer
Device layer: phone, tablet, laptop, sensor
Wireless link: cellular, Wi-Fi or Bluetooth, with limited bandwidth and errors
Fixed network plus middleware that hides mobility and disconnection
Diagram: device → air interface → base station → fixed network → server
Applications: UPI payment from a moving phone, IRCTC booking on a train, field service, ambulance telemetry

bank.q: Trace the evolution from 1G to 5G. For each generation, state the new capability added and the multiple access method used.
outline: 1G: analog voice, FDMA, poor security
2G: digital voice and SMS, GSM uses TDMA, IS-95 uses CDMA
2.5G: GPRS and EDGE add packet data
3G: UMTS and WCDMA, mobile internet with voice and data together
4G: LTE all-IP, OFDMA, flat architecture
5G: NR, wider bandwidth, network slicing, low latency
Table form with generation, year band, data rate order and access method
One line on what stayed the same: the cellular reuse idea

bank.q: Draw the GSM system architecture. Explain the role of MS, BTS, BSC, MSC, HLR and VLR, then explain how GPRS adds packet data.
outline: MS = mobile equipment plus SIM; IMSI identifies the subscriber
BTS is the radio cell, BSC controls several BTS
MSC switches calls and connects to the PSTN; HLR and VLR hold registers
GSM voice path is circuit-switched, set up by signalling before speech
GPRS adds SGSN and GGSN, a packet control unit and PDP context activation
GPRS attach and PDP context request as the two setup steps
UMTS then replaces the radio with WCDMA and adds Node B and RNC

bank.q: Explain frequency reuse in a hexagonal cellular layout. Derive N = i² + ij + j² and Q = D/R = √(3N).
outline: Hexagon chosen because it tiles without gaps and approximates a circle
A cluster of N cells uses all channels once, then repeats
i and j are step counts along the two hexagon axes
N = i² + ij + j² with a worked example such as i = 2, j = 1 giving N = 7
Geometry gives D/R = √(3N)
Large N: more reuse distance, less interference, fewer channels per cell
Small N: more capacity, more interference

bank.q: An operator has 840 channels in total and uses a reuse cluster of N = 7. Find the channels per cell and D/R. Repeat for N = 4 and comment on capacity against interference.
outline: Channels per cell = 840/7 = 120
For N = 4: 840/4 = 210 channels per cell
D/R = √12 ≈ 3.46, so co-channel cells are closer
Capacity per cell rises, carrier-to-interference ratio falls
Conclusion: N is a planned trade-off between capacity and quality

bank.q: A user on a moving train crosses three cells during one call. Describe the handover process step by step and the signalling between MS, BSC and MSC.
outline: MS measures its own and neighbour cell signal strengths and reports them
Serving BSC compares and decides a handover is needed
Handover request to MSC, which asks the target BSC for a channel
Target allocates a traffic channel and returns an acknowledgement
MSC switches the voice path to the new BSC
MS tunes to the new channel and sends handover complete
Old channel released; hysteresis and dwell time prevent ping-pong
Hard handover in GSM, soft handover in CDMA where two links run together

bank.q: A mobile node leaves its home network and attaches to a foreign network. Explain agent discovery, registration and packet delivery, naming every message.
outline: Agent advertisement or agent solicitation finds the foreign agent
MN builds a care-of address, either foreign-agent CoA or co-located CoA
Registration request goes to FA, then to HA; HA updates its binding cache
Registration reply returns to the MN with lifetime
CN sends a packet to the home address; HA intercepts it
HA tunnels the packet to the CoA using IP-in-IP
FA decapsulates and delivers to the MN
Reverse tunneling for replies when ingress filtering is used

bank.q: Explain CSMA/CA in IEEE 802.11 with DIFS, backoff and the RTS/CTS exchange, and show how it deals with the hidden node problem.
outline: Carrier sense plus interframe spacing: SIFS for ACK, DIFS for new transmissions
Random backoff counts down only while the channel is idle
Receiver sends ACK; no ACK means collision, so retransmit
Hidden node: two stations cannot hear each other and both send
RTS from sender and CTS from receiver carry a duration value
Other stations set their NAV and stay silent for that time
Fragmentation threshold and physical versus virtual carrier sense
Contrast with CSMA/CD, which detects collisions instead of avoiding them

bank.q: Five nodes form an ad hoc network with no access point. Explain how a reactive protocol such as AODV discovers a route and repairs it after a link breaks.
outline: Source broadcasts RREQ with destination, sequence number and hop count
Intermediate nodes store a reverse route to the source
Destination replies with a unicast RREP along the reverse path
Forward route entries installed with a lifetime
Data flows; hello messages or link-layer feedback detect a break
A node sends RERR upstream; affected routes are invalidated
New RREQ only when a route is needed, which saves energy
Compare with a proactive protocol, which keeps routes for all nodes all the time

bank.q: Analyse triangle routing in Mobile IP. Evaluate route optimisation as a remedy, including its costs and risks.
outline: Packets go CN → HA → MN even when CN and MN share a foreign network
Costs: extra delay, load on HA, longer path, possible congestion on the home link
Route optimisation: HA sends a binding update to the CN
CN keeps a binding cache and tunnels directly to the CoA
Savings show up as shorter path and lower delay
Costs: binding cache state in every CN, authentication of updates, stale bindings, security against spoofed updates
HA still needed for the first packet and for nodes that do not support it

bank.q: Compare a cellular network, an IEEE 802.11 WLAN and a mobile ad hoc network for three deployments: a metro city, a college campus, and a flood-hit area with no infrastructure. Recommend one for each with reasons.
outline: City: licensed cellular, wide coverage, managed handover, high cost and spectrum licence
Campus: WLAN with access points and backhaul, high data rate, low cost, limited range
Disaster area: MANET, no base station, nodes relay for each other, but limited battery and capacity
Compare coverage, mobility support, bandwidth, delay, energy, cost and reliability
Cellular needs location tracking and handover; WLAN needs CSMA/CA; MANET needs a routing protocol
State the recommendation with the reason, and mention a hybrid such as phones acting as hotspots

bank.q: Compare FDM/TDM cellular systems with cellular CDMA on capacity, reuse, power control and handover.
outline: FDM/TDM: hard reuse factor about 1/7, careful frequency planning
CDMA: reuse factor 1 everywhere, interference limited, soft capacity
Near-far problem makes power control essential in CDMA; TPC loop
Voice activity factor and sectorisation raise CDMA capacity
Soft handover in CDMA versus hard handover in GSM
Erlang capacity comparison and what limits each system
Grade of service and trunking: blocking versus interference limit

bank.q: Analyse how cell size and user speed affect handover rate and location update signalling load. How does the network balance the two?
outline: Higher speed or smaller cells mean more cell crossings per call, so more handovers
More handovers mean more signalling and a higher drop risk
Small cells mean more location updates for idle users but cheaper paging
Large location areas mean few updates but expensive wide paging
Tune the boundary with hysteresis, dwell timers and neighbour lists
Umbrella cells over microcells for fast users
Trade-off stated as a signalling cost balance between update and paging

glossary.def: The fixed radio equipment that serves one cell and connects mobile devices to the network.
Mobile Switching Centre: the exchange that sets up and switches calls in a cellular network.
Subscriber Identity Module: the card that holds the subscriber identity and authenticates it to the network.
International Mobile Subscriber Identity: the unique number stored in the SIM that identifies the subscriber.
Frequency Division Multiple Access: each user is given its own narrow frequency band for the whole call.
Time Division Multiple Access: users share one frequency but transmit in separate time slots.
Code Division Multiple Access: all users share the whole band at once and are separated by spreading codes.
Using a mobile service on a network other than the home network, arranged through inter-operator agreements.
The geographical area covered by one base station antenna, drawn as a hexagon in planning.
The fixed WLAN device that bridges wireless stations to the wired network.
Service Set Identifier: the name that identifies an IEEE 802.11 network.
A Wi-Fi security standard using AES encryption and a key exchange to protect the wireless link.
Two stations that cannot hear each other both transmit to the same receiver and collide.
Request To Send and Clear To Send frames that reserve the medium and silence hidden stations.
A periodic message from a home or foreign agent announcing its presence and care-of address to mobile nodes.
A message a mobile node broadcasts to ask for an immediate agent advertisement.
Wrapping a packet inside another IP packet so it can be delivered to a temporary address.
Removing the outer header of a tunnelled packet to recover the original packet.
Router on the visited network that delivers tunnelled packets to the visiting mobile node.
The host that is communicating with the mobile node.
Informing the correspondent node of the binding so packets can go directly to the care-of address.
Finding a route only when a packet must be sent, as in AODV and DSR.
Keeping routes to all destinations up to date all the time, as in DSDV and OLSR.
Long Term Evolution: the all-IP 4G cellular standard with a flat architecture and OFDMA radio.
